summary: Updates RFC 9048 and RFC 5448 with an optional extension that adds an ephemeral key exchange to EAP-AKA'. When negotiated, it provides forward secrecy for the session keys generated in the authentication, so later key compromise does not expose past sessions.

eli5.summary: Each time your phone logs in, it makes a fresh one-time secret and throws it away. Even if a thief later learns the main password, they cannot unlock old conversations.

subtitle: An optional add-on that gives mobile network logins forward secrecy, so a stolen SIM key cannot unlock past sessions.

tldr.problem: If an attacker obtains the long-term key stored on a USIM card, plain EAP-AKA' lets them work out past session keys and passively read future ones.
tldr.mechanism: EAP-AKA' FS adds an ephemeral elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman exchange, carried in two new optional attributes, and mixes the shared secret into the exported session keys.
tldr.outcome: Past sessions stay protected and attackers must become active to reach future ones, with no new credentials and no extra protocol rounds.

today: RFC 9678 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2025. It updates RFC 9048 and RFC 5448, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. The extension is optional and used at the discretion of the authenticating parties.

sections.title: The Problem: Stolen Long-Term Keys
sections.content:
Reports of pervasive surveillance included attacks on the supply chain of Universal Subscriber Identity Module (USIM) cards. The AKA long-term key could be revealed during card manufacturing, during transfer of cards to the operator, or while the system is running. The RFC stresses that the issue is not weak algorithms but unauthorized access to key material.

This document updates RFC 9048 (and its predecessor RFC 5448) with an optional extension that provides forward secrecy for the session key generated in an EAP-AKA' run. An attacker who gets the long-term key cannot reach past session keys. The Diffie-Hellman exchange also forces attackers to be active to reach future ones, and active attacks cost more and are easier to detect. The text notes that 5G uses the EAP framework and that EAP-AKA' is the default method there.
sections.eli5: The master key on a SIM card is like a skeleton key that thieves would love to copy. This add-on makes sure that even a copied skeleton key cannot open the doors to yesterday's conversations.

sections.title: AKA and EAP-AKA' in Brief
sections.content:
AKA (Authentication and Key Agreement) is the challenge-response protocol used by 3GPP mobile networks from the third generation on. The USIM and the home environment share a long-term symmetric key. The home environment produces an authentication vector containing RAND, AUTN, XRES, a 128-bit integrity key IK and a 128-bit encryption key CK. The USIM checks AUTN and answers with RES.

In EAP-AKA' the server acts as EAP Server and the USIM plus phone act as the peer. The difference from EAP-AKA is that EAP-AKA' binds the derived keys to the name of the access network. The exchange is an identity request and response, an EAP-Request/AKA'-Challenge, an EAP-Response/AKA'-Challenge and finally EAP-Success.
sections.eli5: The phone and the network each prove they know a shared secret by answering a surprise question. Then they use the same secret to make the keys that lock the rest of the conversation.

sections.title: How the Extension Works
sections.content:
Forward secrecy comes from an Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman exchange run in an ephemeral way (ECDHE): both sides generate temporary keys. The Server puts its public key in the first challenge message and the Peer answers with its own. The extension keeps the interface between USIM and phone intact, so no new credentials or card changes are needed, and it does not add rounds to the protocol.

The new data travels in optional, skippable attributes. A peer that does not support the extension ignores them and carries on with plain EAP-AKA' under RFC 9048 rules. The base integrity check still covers the attributes, which helps protect against bidding-down attacks.

Once both public keys are exchanged, the keys exported from the EAP run are based on CK, IK and the ECDHE shared value, rather than on CK and IK alone. So even someone holding the long-term key would have to be an active attacker to determine the session keys.
sections.eli5: Both sides secretly pick a random number, swap a disguised version, and combine them into a shared secret that was never sent. Then they forget their random numbers, so nobody can rebuild the secret later.

sections.title: The New Attributes
sections.content:
Two new attributes are added. AT_PUB_ECDHE (type 152) carries the sender's ECDHE public key. For X25519 the value is 32 bytes, encoded as in RFC 7748. For P-256 it is 33 bytes in compressed form. The sender pads the value with zero bytes to a multiple of 4 bytes and SHALL generate a fresh value for each run of the protocol.

AT_KDF_FS (type 153) names the forward-secrecy key derivation function and, with it, the ECDHE group. Its length MUST be 1. It sits beside AT_KDF, which still carries the basic KDF value for peers that do not use the extension. Two FS KDF values are defined: 1 for "EAP-AKA' with ECDHE and X25519" and 2 for "EAP-AKA' with ECDHE and P-256". Support for both groups is REQUIRED.
sections.eli5: Two new labels are stuck on the message. One carries the disguised secret number, and the other says which secret-making recipe to use.

sections.title: Key Derivation
sections.content:
Keys used inside the authentication run do not change, so AT_MAC keeps working as before. What changes are the re-authentication key and the keys exported from the method. With AT_KDF_FS set to 1 or 2 and AT_KDF set to 1:

MK       = PRF'(IK'|CK',"EAP-AKA'"|Identity)
MK_ECDHE = PRF'(IK'|CK'|SHARED_SECRET,"EAP-AKA' FS"|Identity)
K_encr   = MK[0..127]
K_aut    = MK[128..383]
K_re     = MK_ECDHE[0..255]
MSK      = MK_ECDHE[256..767]
EMSK     = MK_ECDHE[768..1279]

So MK_ECDHE mixes the Diffie-Hellman secret with the AKA keys, and the MSK, EMSK and re-authentication key come from it. At least partial public key validation MUST be done for P-256 ephemeral keys. If validation of the other party's key or the shared secret fails, a party MUST behave as if EAP-AKA' starts again from the beginning.
sections.eli5: The old recipe stirred two ingredients into the key soup. The new recipe also stirs in the secret that only exists for this one login, so the soup cannot be remade later.

sections.title: Negotiation and Message Processing
sections.content:
The Server MUST send one or more AT_KDF_FS attributes in the EAP-Request/AKA'-Challenge, ordered by preference, but includes a public key only for the first one. If the Peer accepts it, the function is used with no further negotiation. If not, the Peer replies with a challenge response containing only AT_KDF_FS naming a different offered function. If there is no suitable alternative, the Peer can fall back to EAP-AKA' or fail the authentication. The Server then re-sends the challenge with the selected function added at the start of the list, and the Peer MUST check that only the requested change occurred.

In the final exchange, the Peer's response includes AT_RES, AT_PUB_ECDHE and AT_MAC. Whether to allow a fallback when one side does not use the extension is a policy decision. A server that does not allow it MUST behave as if authentication failed. Other message types are unchanged, except that the new attributes MUST NOT be added to the identity, synchronization-failure, authentication-reject or client-error messages. The peer identifier SHALL comply with the privacy-friendly requirements of RFC 9190. Re-authentication reuses the keys from the original run and runs no new Diffie-Hellman exchange.
sections.eli5: The network offers a list of secret-making recipes, best first. If the phone prefers another one from the list, it says so, and both agree out loud so nobody can sneak in a weaker choice.

sections.title: Security Properties and Limits
sections.content:
Without ephemeral key exchange, a compromised long-term key lets an attacker decrypt previously recorded 5G communication, passively decrypt all future communication, and impersonate the user equipment or the network. The extension protects past sessions and makes passive monitoring of future ones useless. An active, on-path attacker who holds the long-term key can still eavesdrop on future runs. The RFC recommends phasing out EAP-AKA methods without forward secrecy in the long term.

Forward secrecy only holds if endpoints destroy the ephemeral keys and anything that could recompute them. Negotiation stays protected against bidding-down because the attributes are covered by AT_MAC, except against an attacker who holds the long-term key and is active. Data in AT_ENCR in the first challenge is not forward secret, which could let such an attacker link re-authentication runs that use pseudonyms.

On quantum computers, the RFC says a sufficiently powerful one could recover the shared secret from the public keys, and together with the long-term key this would disable the forward secrecy, though authentication itself would remain safe. It does not add post-quantum algorithms but says a future update can.
sections.eli5: Forget-it-after-use secrets protect old chats, but a burglar who is standing in the room during a new chat can still listen. Making the burglar stand there every time is already much harder for them.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The extension shares its attribute space with EAP-SIM (RFC 4186), EAP-AKA (RFC 4187) and EAP-AKA' (RFC 9048). IANA assigned AT_PUB_ECDHE as 152 and AT_KDF_FS as 153 in the skippable attribute range 128-255.

IANA also created the "EAP-AKA' AT_KDF_FS Key Derivation Function Values" registry. Value 0 is reserved, 1 and 2 are the X25519 and P-256 types, and 3-65535 are unassigned. New values need the Specification Required policy.
sections.eli5: A public list of numbers was updated so that everyone uses the same number for each new label.
